4. // PhysicalAddress — Specifications
5. //
6. // A `PhysicalAddress` abstracts to a single mathematical integer: the raw
7. // physical address (`PhysicalAddress@ : int`, defined by the `View` impl in
8. // `phys.rs`, delegating to the inner `VirtualAddress`). The only derived notion
9. // callers reason about is the *frame* the address lies in
10. // (`addr / FRAME_SIZE == addr >> FRAME_SHIFT`), used to index the frame
11. // allocator's bitmaps / refcount arrays.
12. //
13. // Trust-boundary helpers pin the not-yet-verified `arch` `FrameNumber` type and
14. // the `arch`/`sys` library-edge constants/methods this module calls. They mirror
15. // the existing `sys`/`arch` `assume_specification` boundaries the codebase
16. // already draws (`::arch::mem::PAGE_SIZE` in `frame.rs`, the `Address` trait
17. // methods in `page.spec.rs` / `kframe.spec.rs`). `spec_page_size()` is the
18. // canonical frame size, re-exported from `crate::hal::mem` (defined alongside
19. // `FrameAddress`); `FRAME_SIZE == PAGE_SIZE == spec_page_size()`.
20. 
21. verus! {
22. 
23. use crate::hal::mem::spec_page_size;
24. use vstd::arithmetic::power2::pow2;
25. use vstd::arithmetic::div_mod::{
26.     lemma_fundamental_div_mod,
27.     lemma_mod_division_less_than_divisor,
28.     lemma_div_by_multiple,
29.     lemma_mod_multiples_basic,
30. };
31. use vstd::bits::lemma_usize_shr_is_div;
32. 
33. // `FrameNumber` lives in the `arch` crate, which is not Verus-enabled and has no
34. // `View`/datatype registration reachable here. Declare it to Verus as an opaque
35. // external datatype so it may appear in spec-fn parameters and the
36. // `assume_specification`s below. Its internals are not modeled (`external_body`):
37. // its abstract index is projected by `spec_frame_raw_value`.
38. #[verifier::external_type_specification]
39. #[verifier::external_body]
40. pub struct ExFrameNumber(FrameNumber);
41. 
42. // ── Frame-number trust-boundary projections (arch `FrameNumber`) ──────────────
43. //
44. // `FrameNumber` lives in the `arch` crate, which is not Verus-enabled and has no
45. // `View` impl reachable here (orphan rule). Its abstract index is therefore
46. // projected by an uninterpreted ghost function, exactly as `view_design.md`
47. // prescribes. `spec_max_frame_number()` denotes `FrameNumber::MAX`.
48. 
49. // The integer index of a frame number (`0 ..= spec_max_frame_number()`).
50. pub uninterp spec fn spec_frame_raw_value(frame: FrameNumber) -> int;
51. 
52. // The largest representable frame number. Mirrors `arch FrameNumber::MAX ==
53. // MAX_ADDRESS / FRAME_SIZE - 1 == usize::MAX / FRAME_SIZE - 1`. Interpreting it
54. // against `usize::MAX` and `spec_page_size()` is what lets verified constructors
55. // discharge their `usize` multiply (no-overflow) obligation: a frame index in
56. // `0 ..= spec_max_frame_number()` scaled by `spec_page_size()` stays `<= usize::MAX`.
57. pub open spec fn spec_max_frame_number() -> int {
58.     usize::MAX as int / spec_page_size() - 1
59. }
60. 
61. // ── Derived spec helpers over the View domain (`int`) ─────────────────────────
62. 
63. // The frame an address lies in: exact integer division, independent of whether
64. // the implementation shifts (`>> FRAME_SHIFT`) or divides (`/ FRAME_SIZE`).
65. pub open spec fn spec_frame_number(addr_view: int) -> int {
66.     addr_view / spec_page_size()
67. }
68. 
69. // The base (frame-aligned) address of a frame index: `frame * FRAME_SIZE`.
70. pub open spec fn spec_from_number(frame_view: int) -> int {
71.     frame_view * spec_page_size()
72. }
73. 
74. // ── `arch`/`sys` library-edge `assume_specification`s ─────────────────────────
75. 
76. // `::arch::mem::FRAME_SIZE` is the frame size (alias of `PAGE_SIZE`), tied to the
77. // canonical `spec_page_size()`. It is strictly positive (`== 4096`); positivity is
78. // the load-bearing fact for the division/modulo reasoning in the constructors.
79. pub assume_specification[ ::arch::mem::FRAME_SIZE ] -> (result: usize)
80.     ensures
81.         result == spec_page_size(),
82.         spec_page_size() > 0,
83. ;
84. 
85. // `::arch::mem::FRAME_SHIFT == log2(FRAME_SIZE)`. Bounded below the pointer width
86. // so `raw_addr >> FRAME_SHIFT` is well-defined, and `2^FRAME_SHIFT == FRAME_SIZE`
87. // so the shift coincides with division by `spec_page_size()`.
88. pub assume_specification[ ::arch::mem::FRAME_SHIFT ] -> (result: usize)
89.     ensures
90.         result < usize::BITS,
91.         pow2(result as nat) == spec_page_size(),
92. ;
93. 
94. // `VirtualAddress::new` is a pure newtype constructor: the wrapped value is the
95. // abstract address. (`sys` library edge; the inner module is not yet verified.)
96. pub assume_specification[ VirtualAddress::new ](value: usize) -> (result: VirtualAddress)
97.     ensures
98.         result@ == value as int,
99. ;
100. 
101. // `<VirtualAddress as Address>::into_raw_value` is pure newtype identity: the
102. // returned raw `usize` equals the abstract address.
103. pub assume_specification[ <VirtualAddress as Address>::into_raw_value ](
104.     addr: VirtualAddress,
105. ) -> (result: usize)
106.     ensures
107.         result as int == addr@,
108. ;
109. 
110. // `FrameNumber::into_raw_value` projects a frame number to its index; every
111. // `FrameNumber` value is in range (`0 ..= MAX`) by construction.
112. pub assume_specification[ FrameNumber::into_raw_value ](frame: FrameNumber) -> (result: usize)
113.     ensures
114.         result as int == spec_frame_raw_value(frame),
115.         0 <= spec_frame_raw_value(frame) <= spec_max_frame_number(),
116. ;
117. 
118. // `FrameNumber::from_raw_value` succeeds iff `value <= MAX`, preserving the index.
119. pub assume_specification[ FrameNumber::from_raw_value ](value: usize) -> (result: Option<FrameNumber>)
120.     ensures
121.         match result {
122.             Some(f) => value as int <= spec_max_frame_number()
123.                 && spec_frame_raw_value(f) == value as int,
124.             None => value as int > spec_max_frame_number(),
125.         },
126. ;

128. // ── Type invariant ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
129. //
130. // Every `PhysicalAddress` a verified constructor produces has a *representable
131. // frame number*: `self@ / FRAME_SIZE <= FrameNumber::MAX`. This is the load-
132. // bearing fact that makes `into_frame_number` total (its internal
133. // `FrameNumber::from_raw_value(..).unwrap()` never panics), which the frame
134. // allocator relies on when using the result directly as a bitmap / refcount
135. // index. It is *not* alignment (MMIO addresses may be unaligned) and *not*
136. // RAM-validity (`from_mmio_address` deliberately bypasses that check).

# Caller Analysis: `hal::mem::types::address::phys` (`PhysicalAddress`)

## Script Output

See: `verus-ai-logs/nanvix-phys-hal-phys-address/find_callers_lsp_output.md`
(raw `find_callers_lsp.py` output — intra-crate, rust-analyzer LSP, crate `kernel`).

Module is leaf within the `kernel` crate: **no external crates depend on it**, so all
callers are intra-crate. The script reports 16 exec functions (all pub / trait-pub),
0 private, 1 type. This analysis focuses on the **verification-order target functions**:

- `PhysicalAddress` (the type)
- `PhysicalAddress::from_number`
- `PhysicalAddress::into_frame_number`
- `PhysicalAddress::from_mmio_address`

## Pre-existing Specs (from upstream verification)

- `phys.spec.rs` and `phys.proof.rs` exist but are **empty** (`verus! { }`).
- Functions with specs: **none**.
- View type: **does not exist** in the spec files. (A `closed spec fn view(&self) -> int`
  returning `self.0@` is defined inline in `phys.rs` under `verus_keep_ghost`, i.e. the
  physical address abstracts to the underlying virtual address's integer value.)
- Assessment: clean slate. No upstream caller has biased the View yet; the inline
  `View::V = int` (raw address as a mathematical integer) is the natural starting point
  and is consistent with how callers use the type (see below).

## Trait Obligations

`PhysicalAddress` implements:

- `Address` (`from_raw_value`, `align_up`, `align_down`, `is_aligned`, `max_addr`,
  `into_raw_value`, `as_ptr`, `as_mut_ptr`) — generic address contract. Used by generic
  code such as `PageAligned<T: Address>` (`from_address`, `PartialEq`, `PartialOrd`),
  which is the primary indirect consumer of `is_aligned`/`into_raw_value`.
- `Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord` — value semantics; callers freely copy
  and compare physical addresses and order them as raw integers.
- `core::fmt::Debug` — delegates to inner `VirtualAddress`; callers only expect a
  human-readable hex dump (logging in `book`, boot_init, `mod.rs`).

Key trait-mediated expectation: `into_frame_number` / `from_number` and
`PageAligned::from_address` together rely on the `Address::is_aligned` contract — a
physical address built from a frame number is page-aligned, so wrapping it in
`PageAligned` cannot fail.

## Caller Expectations

### `PhysicalAddress` (the type) — 76 references

Representative callers: `mm/phys/frame.rs` (frame allocator: `book`, `is_covered`,
`alloc_range` take `PageAligned<PhysicalAddress>` / `TruncatedMemoryRegion<PhysicalAddress>`),
`mm/phys/mod.rs`, `kmod.rs` (stores `start` / `region_base` as `PhysicalAddress`),
`hal/mem/types/address/frame.rs` (`FrameAddress` wraps `PageAligned<PhysicalAddress>`).

- **Callers assume:**
  - It is a cheap `Copy` value that abstracts to a single integer (the raw physical
    address). Equality/ordering match integer equality/ordering of that raw value.
  - A `PhysicalAddress` that exists is a *valid* physical address (constructors enforce
    validity via `is_valid_physical_address`, except the explicitly-unsafe MMIO path).
  - Round-trips with `FrameNumber` and `usize` preserve the underlying value.
- **Callers don't care about:**
  - That the inner representation is a `VirtualAddress` newtype. They never see the inner
    type; they go through `into_raw_value` / `into_virtual_address` / frame conversions.
  - Any platform-specific validity range internals.

### `from_number(frame: FrameNumber) -> Self`

Sole caller: `hal/mem/types/address/frame.rs:78`
`Ok(Self(PageAligned::from_address(PhysicalAddress::from_number(frame_number))?))`
(inside `FrameAddress::from_frame_number`).

- **Callers assume (success — infallible, returns `Self` not `Result`):**
  - The produced address equals `frame * FRAME_SIZE`, i.e. it is **page-aligned**. This
    is load-bearing: the caller immediately feeds the result to
    `PageAligned::from_address`, which calls `is_aligned(PAGE_ALIGNMENT)` and would error
    on a misaligned address. The caller propagates that `?` but in practice expects it to
    never trip for a frame-number-derived address.
  - The result is a valid, in-range physical address for any well-formed `FrameNumber`
    (`FrameNumber` is constructed only within `0..=MAX`, where `MAX = MAX_ADDRESS/FRAME_SIZE - 1`).
  - It is the inverse of `into_frame_number`: `from_number(f).into_frame_number() == f`.
- **Callers don't care about:**
  - That it multiplies by `FRAME_SIZE` vs shifts by `FRAME_SHIFT` internally, or that it
    wraps a `VirtualAddress::new`.
- **Would break the caller if changed:** returning a non-page-aligned address, or an
  address not equal to `frame * FRAME_SIZE` (breaks the `PageAligned` wrap and the
  round-trip with `into_frame_number`).

### `into_frame_number(self) -> FrameNumber`

Callers (4):
- `hal/mem/types/address/frame.rs:82` — `FrameAddress::into_frame_number` delegates.
- `mm/phys/frame.rs:482` (`book`), `:518` (`is_covered`), `:569` (`alloc_range`):
  `let frame_number: usize = phys_addr.into_frame_number().into_raw_value();`
  then used to index a bitmap / refcount array.

- **Callers assume (success — infallible, total):**

# View Design: `PhysicalAddress` (`hal/mem/types/address/phys.rs`)

> Scope: design the abstract `View` (+ `inv`) for `PhysicalAddress` that the
> in-scope functions will reference in later spec/proof phases.
>
> In-scope (verification-order) targets: the type `PhysicalAddress` (its `View`
> and `inv`), `PhysicalAddress::from_number`, `PhysicalAddress::into_frame_number`,
> and `PhysicalAddress::from_mmio_address`. Every other item — the full `Address`
> trait impl (`from_raw_value`, `align_up/down`, `is_aligned`, `max_addr`,
> `into_raw_value`, `as_ptr`/`as_mut_ptr`), `from_virtual_address`,
> `into_virtual_address`, `from_frame_address`, `from_into_frame_address`, and
> `Debug::fmt` — is **out of scope** and untouched.
>
> A scalar `View` skeleton (`type V = int; view(&self) = self.0@`) already exists
> inline in the module's `verus!` block. This document **reviews and confirms**
> that skeleton against the caller analysis, applies the substitution test to
> each candidate field, and designs the `inv()` and the spec transitions the
> in-scope contracts will use.

---

## Abstract Resource

`PhysicalAddress` is, to its callers, **an opaque integer identifier for a single
byte location in guest-physical memory** — a validated handle whose only
observable state is one mathematical integer, the **raw physical address**.

It is the currency exchanged between the frame allocator (`mm/phys/frame.rs`),
the paging / boot-init code (`mm/virt/boot_init.rs`, `mm/phys/mod.rs`), kernel
module descriptors (`kmod.rs`), and the frame-granular wrappers
(`PageAligned<PhysicalAddress>`, `FrameAddress`). From that single integer every
caller derives the one further concept it ever needs: the **frame** the address
lies in (`addr >> FRAME_SHIFT == addr / FRAME_SIZE`), used to index bitmaps and
refcount arrays and to encode PTE/PDE frame fields.

It is **not** a collection, resource manager, or state machine: it is an
immutable, `Copy`, totally-ordered scalar value whose equality and ordering agree
with integer equality/ordering of the raw address. That it is internally a
newtype over `VirtualAddress` is invisible to callers — the caller analysis is
explicit: callers "don't care that the inner representation is a `VirtualAddress`
newtype … they go through `into_raw_value` / `into_virtual_address` / frame
conversions."

---

## View Struct

The abstract state of a `PhysicalAddress` is **exactly one value**: the raw
numeric address as an unbounded integer. Verus models this with a scalar `View`
(`type V = int`), not a one-field record, because there is only one
caller-observable quantity. The existing inline skeleton is **kept unchanged**:

```rust
impl View for PhysicalAddress {
    type V = int;

    // `closed`: callers may reference `self@`, but the mapping to the inner
    // VirtualAddress field is hidden. The abstract value is "the physical
    // address as an unbounded integer".
    closed spec fn view(&self) -> int {
        self.0@      // newtype identity: delegate to the inner address's view
    }
}
```

`self@ : int` is the entire abstract state. This mirrors the rest of the address
tower — `VirtualAddress@ : int`, `PageAligned<T>@ : int`, `FrameAddress@ : int`,
`FrameNumber@ : int` — confirming the abstraction is caller-driven, not
implementation-driven: every member models a value as a single `int`.

`view()` is **`closed`** so the newtype delegation (`self.0@`) does not leak the
`VirtualAddress` representation; callers still obtain a usable `int` (`p@`) for
arithmetic, frame indexing, and comparison.

### Equivalent "single-field" reading

```rust
pub struct PhysicalAddressView {
    // addr: the numeric physical address this handle denotes, as `int`.
    //       The only state a caller can observe. The "frame it lies in" is a
    //       *derived* quantity (addr / FRAME_SIZE), not a stored field;
    //       in-range-ness is a *property* of this value, expressed by inv().
    addr: int,
}
```

### Derived spec helper (over the View domain)

The frame index is the single derived quantity callers reason about, so it gets a
named helper over the abstract `int` rather than a stored field:

```rust
// The frame that this physical address belongs to. Equals the implementation's
// `addr >> FRAME_SHIFT`, stated as exact integer division so the spec is
// independent of shift-vs-divide.
pub open spec fn spec_frame_number(addr_view: int) -> int {
    addr_view / spec_page_size()
}
```

`spec_page_size() : int` is the pre-existing uninterpreted module constant tied
to `FRAME_SIZE`/`PAGE_SIZE` (the caller analysis establishes
`FRAME_SIZE == spec_page_size()`). `spec_max_frame_number() : int` denotes
`FrameNumber::MAX` (`= MAX_ADDRESS / FRAME_SIZE - 1`); together with
`spec_frame_raw_value(frame: FrameNumber) -> int` (the frame's integer index)
these are the trust-boundary helpers that pin the not-yet-verified `arch`
`FrameNumber` type at the `phys.spec.rs` edge, and they are the vocabulary the
`from_number` / `into_frame_number` contracts use.

---

## Well-formedness Invariant

`PhysicalAddress` carries **one** universal property that every constructible
value satisfies and that callers depend on: its address has a **representable
frame number**. This is exactly the fact that makes `into_frame_number` total —
its internal `FrameNumber::from_raw_value(addr >> FRAME_SHIFT).unwrap()` never
panics — which the frame allocator relies on to use the result directly as a
bitmap / refcount index without a bounds re-check.

171.             assert(fr * p <= m) by (nonlinear_arith)
172.                 requires

174.                     fr >= 0,
175.                     fr <= m / p - 1,
176.                     p * (m / p) <= m,
177.             ;
178.         }

4. // PhysicalAddress — Specifications
5. //
6. // A `PhysicalAddress` abstracts to a single mathematical integer: the raw
7. // physical address (`PhysicalAddress@ : int`, defined by the `View` impl in
8. // `phys.rs`, delegating to the inner `VirtualAddress`). The only derived notion
9. // callers reason about is the *frame* the address lies in
10. // (`addr / FRAME_SIZE == addr >> FRAME_SHIFT`), used to index the frame
11. // allocator's bitmaps / refcount arrays.
12. //
13. // Trust-boundary helpers pin the not-yet-verified `arch` `FrameNumber` type and
14. // the `arch`/`sys` library-edge constants/methods this module calls. They mirror
15. // the existing `sys`/`arch` `assume_specification` boundaries the codebase
16. // already draws (`::arch::mem::PAGE_SIZE` in `frame.rs`, the `Address` trait
17. // methods in `page.spec.rs` / `kframe.spec.rs`). `spec_page_size()` is the
18. // canonical frame size, re-exported from `crate::hal::mem` (defined alongside
19. // `FrameAddress`); `FRAME_SIZE == PAGE_SIZE == spec_page_size()`.
20.

22. 
23. use crate::hal::mem::spec_page_size;
24. use vstd::arithmetic::power2::pow2;
25. use vstd::arithmetic::div_mod::{
26.     lemma_fundamental_div_mod,
27.     lemma_mod_division_less_than_divisor,
28.     lemma_div_by_multiple,
29.     lemma_mod_multiples_basic,
30. };
31. use vstd::bits::lemma_usize_shr_is_div;
32. 
33. // `FrameNumber` lives in the `arch` crate, which is not Verus-enabled and has no
34. // `View`/datatype registration reachable here. Declare it to Verus as an opaque
35. // external datatype so it may appear in spec-fn parameters and the
36. // `assume_specification`s below. Its internals are not modeled (`external_body`):
37. // its abstract index is projected by `spec_frame_raw_value`.
38. #[verifier::external_type_specification]
39. #[verifier::external_body]
40. pub struct ExFrameNumber(FrameNumber);
41. 
42. // ── Frame-number trust-boundary projections (arch `FrameNumber`) ──────────────
43. //
44. // `FrameNumber` lives in the `arch` crate, which is not Verus-enabled and has no
45. // `View` impl reachable here (orphan rule). Its abstract index is therefore
46. // projected by an uninterpreted ghost function, exactly as `view_design.md`
47. // prescribes. `spec_max_frame_number()` denotes `FrameNumber::MAX`.
48. 
49. // The integer index of a frame number (`0 ..= spec_max_frame_number()`).
50. pub uninterp spec fn spec_frame_raw_value(frame: FrameNumber) -> int;
51. 
52. // The largest representable frame number. Mirrors `arch FrameNumber::MAX ==
53. // MAX_ADDRESS / FRAME_SIZE - 1 == usize::MAX / FRAME_SIZE - 1`. Interpreting it
54. // against `usize::MAX` and `spec_page_size()` is what lets verified constructors
55. // discharge their `usize` multiply (no-overflow) obligation: a frame index in
56. // `0 ..= spec_max_frame_number()` scaled by `spec_page_size()` stays `<= usize::MAX`.
57. pub open spec fn spec_max_frame_number() -> int {
58.     usize::MAX as int / spec_page_size() - 1
59. }
60. 
61. // ── Derived spec helpers over the View domain (`int`) ─────────────────────────
62. 
63. // The frame an address lies in: exact integer division, independent of whether
64. // the implementation shifts (`>> FRAME_SHIFT`) or divides (`/ FRAME_SIZE`).
65. pub open spec fn spec_frame_number(addr_view: int) -> int {
66.     addr_view / spec_page_size()
67. }
68. 
69. // The base (frame-aligned) address of a frame index: `frame * FRAME_SIZE`.
70. pub open spec fn spec_from_number(frame_view: int) -> int {
71.     frame_view * spec_page_size()
72. }
73. 
74. // ── `arch`/`sys` library-edge `assume_specification`s ─────────────────────────
75. 
76. // `::arch::mem::FRAME_SIZE` is the frame size (alias of `PAGE_SIZE`), tied to the
77. // canonical `spec_page_size()`. It is strictly positive (`== 4096`); positivity is
78. // the load-bearing fact for the division/modulo reasoning in the constructors.
79. pub assume_specification[ ::arch::mem::FRAME_SIZE ] -> (result: usize)
80.     ensures
81.         result == spec_page_size(),
82.         spec_page_size() > 0,
83. ;
84. 
85. // `::arch::mem::FRAME_SHIFT == log2(FRAME_SIZE)`. Bounded below the pointer width
86. // so `raw_addr >> FRAME_SHIFT` is well-defined, and `2^FRAME_SHIFT == FRAME_SIZE`
87. // so the shift coincides with division by `spec_page_size()`.
88. pub assume_specification[ ::arch::mem::FRAME_SHIFT ] -> (result: usize)
89.     ensures
90.         result < usize::BITS,
91.         pow2(result as nat) == spec_page_size(),
92. ;
93. 
94. // `VirtualAddress::new` is a pure newtype constructor: the wrapped value is the
95. // abstract address. (`sys` library edge; the inner module is not yet verified.)
96. pub assume_specification[ VirtualAddress::new ](value: usize) -> (result: VirtualAddress)
97.     ensures
98.         result@ == value as int,
99. ;
100. 
101. // `<VirtualAddress as Address>::into_raw_value` is pure newtype identity: the
102. // returned raw `usize` equals the abstract address.
103. pub assume_specification[ <VirtualAddress as Address>::into_raw_value ](
104.     addr: VirtualAddress,
105. ) -> (result: usize)
106.     ensures
107.         result as int == addr@,
108. ;
109. 
110. // `FrameNumber::into_raw_value` projects a frame number to its index; every
111. // `FrameNumber` value is in range (`0 ..= MAX`) by construction.
112. pub assume_specification[ FrameNumber::into_raw_value ](frame: FrameNumber) -> (result: usize)
113.     ensures
114.         result as int == spec_frame_raw_value(frame),
115.         0 <= spec_frame_raw_value(frame) <= spec_max_frame_number(),
116. ;
117. 
118. // `FrameNumber::from_raw_value` succeeds iff `value <= MAX`, preserving the index.
119. pub assume_specification[ FrameNumber::from_raw_value ](value: usize) -> (result: Option<FrameNumber>)
120.     ensures
121.         match result {
122.             Some(f) => value as int <= spec_max_frame_number()
123.                 && spec_frame_raw_value(f) == value as int,
124.             None => value as int > spec_max_frame_number(),
125.         },
126. ;
127. 
128. // ── Type invariant ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
129. //
130. // Every `PhysicalAddress` a verified constructor produces has a *representable
131. // frame number*: `self@ / FRAME_SIZE <= FrameNumber::MAX`. This is the load-
132. // bearing fact that makes `into_frame_number` total (its internal
133. // `FrameNumber::from_raw_value(..).unwrap()` never panics), which the frame
134. // allocator relies on when using the result directly as a bitmap / refcount
135. // index. It is *not* alignment (MMIO addresses may be unaligned) and *not*
136. // RAM-validity (`from_mmio_address` deliberately bypasses that check).
137. impl PhysicalAddress {
138.     pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
139.         spec_frame_number(self@) <= spec_max_frame_number()
140.     }
141. }
142.

144. // address, delegated from the inner `VirtualAddress`. Kept here (verification
145. // material) rather than in `phys.rs` so the exec source carries no cfg-gated
146. // verification constructs.

148.     type V = int;
149. 
150.     closed spec fn view(&self) -> int {
151.         self.0@
152.     }
153. }
154.

 !method_impls.contains(&p)`) on this generic trait impl. It is therefore specced with
 `assume_specification` in `page.spec.rs`, mirroring the existing
 `<PageAligned<T> as Address>::from_raw_value` trust boundary (`kframe.spec.rs`) and the

 `<T as Address>::into_raw_value` newtype identity, discharged when the `Address` trait
 is verified.

   (declared in `src/kernel/src/hal/mem/types/address/aligned/page.spec.rs`).

3. description: "AST-level exec fidelity checking tools and pre-approved deviations. Use after modifying source files to verify exec code is unchanged."
4. ---
5. 
6. # AST Consistency Check
7. 
8. Source exec code must not change during verification — see `verus-constraints`
9. for the full rules. This skill covers the **tooling** to enforce that guarantee.
10. 
11. ## Tools
12. 
13. The checker uses tree-sitter to hash exec code after stripping all
14. ghost/proof/spec annotations. It detects changes invisible to textual diff.
15. 
16. `scripts/ast_consistency.py` provides four subcommands:
17. - `count` — quick pass/fail
18. - `summary` — per-element status table
19. - `diff --name "Fn::name"` — unified diff for one function/struct
20. - `report -o <dir>` — full report with all diffs
21. 
22. The `source` argument is optional. Use `--base-ref` to extract the original
23. from git, or omit both on `verus-ai/*` branches for auto-detection:
24. 
25. ```bash
26. # Explicit original file:
27. python3 scripts/ast_consistency.py original.rs verified.rs count
28. 
29. # Via git ref:
30. python3 scripts/ast_consistency.py --base-ref main verified.rs count
31. 
32. # Auto-detect on verus-ai/* branches:
33. python3 scripts/ast_consistency.py verified.rs count
34. ```
35. 
36. `diff` with `--full` shows specs; default is exec-only.
37. 
38. **MCP alternative**: If the `verus-ast` MCP server is registered, the same
39. functionality is available as tools (`ast_count`, `ast_summary`, `ast_diff`,
40. `ast_report`) with the same auto-detection.
41. 
42. ## Pre-Approved Deviations
43. 
44. These minimal exec changes are known Verus limitations — no full deviation
45. process needed, but still document with a comment:
46. 
47. | Original | Verus Version | Reason |
48. |----------|--------------|--------|
49. | `self.x += 1` | `self.x = self.x + 1` | Compound assignment unsupported |
50. | `self.arr[i] \|= v` | `self.arr.set(i, self.arr[i] \| v)` | Mutable index unsupported |
51. | `-> T` | `-> (ret: T)` | Named returns for ensures |
52. | `#[derive(Clone, ...)]` | `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))] #[derive(...)]` | cfg-gating incompatible derives |
53. | `Ok(Self { .. })` | `let result = Self { .. }; Ok(result)` | Ensures needs to reference return value |
54. | `f(complex_expr)` | `let x = complex_expr; f(x)` | Intermediate value for assertions |
55. | `.ok_or_else(\|\| ...)` | `match ... { Some(v) => v, None => return Err(...) }` | Closures unsupported in some contexts |
56. | `v.std_method(args)` | `wrapper(&mut v, args)` | `&mut T` method unsupported; see `verus-constraints` skill for wrapper rules |
57. 
58. ### Bug Fix Deviations
59. 
60. Exec changes that fix verified bugs are also pre-approved. These must:
61. - Have a `// VERUS BUG FIX: <description>` comment at the fix site
62. - Be recorded in `bugs.md` with full evidence
63. - Be committed with `[verus-ai] BUG FIX:` prefix
64. - Be limited to auto-fixable categories (overflow, off-by-one, missing
65.   bounds check, unchecked cast) — see `bug-reporting` skill
66. 
67. ## Handling MISMATCHes
68. 
69. When the checker reports a MISMATCH:
70. 
71. 1. **Default: restore original code.** Exec changes are violations. Use
72.    `git show <base_ref>:path/to/file.rs` to view the original, then
73.    manually restore the changed exec code while keeping your annotations.
74.    Adapt the proof to the original code — not the other way around.
75. 2. **Check pre-approved deviations.** If the change matches one above,
76.    keep it but add a comment documenting which deviation and why.
77. 3. **Verify it's a real Verus limitation.** Before accepting any other
78.    change, confirm Verus genuinely cannot handle the original construct:
79.    - Search vstd for existing support (e.g. `checked_mul` has vstd specs)
80.    - Try alternative proof strategies that preserve the original code
81.    - Build a minimal reproducer proving the limitation
82. 4. **If confirmed, document with full evidence.** Add a `VERUS DEVIATION`
83.    comment explaining: what was changed, why the original doesn't work,
84.    what alternatives were tried, and why this is the smallest possible change.
85.

1. ---
2. name: verus-constraints
3. description: "Mandatory rules for writing Verus code. Covers attribute-based syntax, source integrity for exec code, forbidden patterns, and assume_specification policy. Must be followed whenever producing or modifying Verus-annotated code."
4. ---
5. 
6. # Verus Constraints
7. 
8. ## Attribute Style for Exec Functions
9. 
10. All specs on **exec functions** must use the attribute-based syntax
11. (`#[verus_spec]`, `#[verus_verify]`, `proof! { }`, `proof_decl! { }`).
12. See the **verus-syntax** skill for the full reference and examples.
13. 
14. ```rust
15. // ✅ CORRECT — attribute style for exec functions
16. #[verus_spec(ret =>
17.     requires x < 100,
18.     ensures ret == x + 1,
19. )]
20. fn foo(x: u32) -> u32 {
21.     x + 1
22. }
23. 
24. // ❌ WRONG — do not wrap exec functions in verus! { }
25. verus! {
26.     fn foo(x: u32) -> (ret: u32)
27.         requires x < 100,
28.         ensures ret == x + 1,
29.     { x + 1 }
30. } // verus!
31. ```
32. 
33. **`verus! { }` blocks** are still used for:
34. - `spec fn` and `proof fn` definitions (in `.spec.rs` and `.proof.rs`)
35. - Type-level specs (`broadcast`, `impl View`, etc.)
36. 
37. Key benefit: exec function signatures stay unmodified — the original `fn`
38. signature is untouched, specs live in the attribute.
39. 
40. ## Source Integrity (exec code)
41. 
42. The following rules apply to the original source files (e.g. `lib.rs`), not to
43. `*.spec.rs` / `*.proof.rs` which are freely editable.
44. 
45. Verus verification is **in-place**: specs and proofs are added directly alongside
46. exec code. The annotated code remains fully compilable and runnable — Verus
47. constructs are erased during normal `cargo build` via cfg-gating. Keep changes
48. minimal so developers can review diffs easily.
49. 
50. **Preserve by default:** exec logic, function signatures, struct definitions,
51. comments, debug assertions, and all other existing code.
52. 
53. The escalation ladder (each step requires exhausting the previous):
54. 
55. 1. **Verify as-is** — most code works with Verus directly.
56. 2. **Search vstd** — your training data is likely outdated. `grep -r` the entire
57.    vstd directory broadly (see "vstd & Common Misconceptions" section below).
58. 3. If verification still fails after steps 1–2, try different proof
59.    strategies (add lemmas, intermediate assertions, split into smaller
60.    functions). If Verus reports that a **syntax construct is unsupported**
61.    (not a proof failure and not a missing spec for a stdlib function),
62.    record it in `verus-unsupported.md` with the exact error message and
63.    the minimal code that triggers it. Do NOT rewrite exec code, add
64.    `external_body`, or add `assume_specification` to work around it.
65. 
66. **The exec code has been pre-refactored to be fully compatible with Verus.**
67. There are no known Verus front-end limitations in the codebase. Any
68. verification failure is a proof issue, not a Verus limitation. Do NOT
69. rewrite exec code, add `external_body` — these are never needed.
70. 
71. **Never cfg-gate away and duplicate exec definitions.** Adding
72. `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` to a function, impl block, struct, enum, or
73. constant and providing a verus-annotated copy is forbidden — it verifies the
74. copy, not the real code, and the two will silently diverge.
75. 
76. - **Functions / impl blocks**: add contracts to the original in-place.
77. - **Structs / enums**: Verus sees the original definition directly. If a
78.   derive macro is incompatible, cfg-gate only the derive attribute, not
79.   the struct. If the struct truly cannot be parsed by Verus, use
80.   `external_type_specification` in spec.rs to declare it — do not
81.   duplicate the definition. Write `external_type_specification` **once**
82.   in the crate/module that defines the type; other modules `use` it.
83. - **Constants**: Verus sees the original definition directly. If Verus
84.   cannot resolve a constant from another workspace module, add
85.   `#[verus_verify]` to the defining module. Never
86.   `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` the original constant.
87. 
88. **Allowed additions:** `#[verus_spec(...)]` and `#[verus_verify]` attributes,
89. `proof! { }` / `proof_decl! { }` / `proof_with! { }` macros, `#[verus_spec(...)]`
90. on loops, `verus! { }` blocks (for spec/proof fn in .spec.rs/.proof.rs),
91. vstd imports (cfg-gated), ghost/tracked local variables (each must be
92. used by at least one proof construct — assertion, invariant, or proof block),
93. `Ghost<T>` / `Tracked<T>` struct fields (only when proof requires ghost
94. state to flow through exec code — prefer keeping ghost state in View),
95. `#[cfg_attr(not(verus_keep_ghost), derive(...))]` gating.
96. 
97. **After completing all changes**, use the `ast-consistency` skill to verify
98. source integrity. Fix all inconsistencies.
99. 
100. ## Forbidden Patterns
101. 
102. | Pattern | Policy |
103. |---|---|
104. | `admit()` | Allowed during specification phase as a placeholder. Must be eliminated during proving phase |
105. | `assume(...)` | Banned |
106. | `#[verifier::external_body]` | **On current module's own functions**: unconditionally forbidden in all phases — `admit()` in a proof body is the correct placeholder during specification (it skips only the proof obligation while Verus still checks exec code; `external_body` skips everything). **On dependency functions in other modules**: allowed as a temporary contract placeholder while the dependency is not yet verified. Must be removed when the dependency module is verified |
107. | `#[verifier::trusted]` | Banned |
108. | `#[verifier::external]` | Banned — not needed under attribute style (only `#[verus_verify]`-annotated items are checked) |
109. | `#[verifier::exec_allows_no_decreases_clause]` | Banned |
110. | `#[verifier::spinoff_prover]` | Banned — even if verification passes with spinoff, the proof is fragile and will break with minor changes. Improve the proof itself |
111. | `#[verifier::rlimit(N)]` | Timeout means the proof is too weak — simplify the proof, split lemmas, add intermediate assertions. Never use rlimit to work around timeouts. If all proof strategies are exhausted and the proof is genuinely optimal, rlimit up to 50 is the absolute maximum |
112. | `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` on exec code | **Cheating** — cfg-gating branches, expressions, match arms, or code blocks means Verus verifies different code than what runs. Only allowed on non-semantic items: `derive(...)`, `debug_assert!`, logging macros (`info!`, `error!`), and imports |
113. | `uninterp spec fn` | **Banned** — all spec functions must have concrete definitions. Using `uninterp` to avoid writing a concrete spec is cheating — it has the same effect as `assume` when paired with `external_body` proof axioms |
114.

116.

     requires x < 100,

         ensures ret == x + 1,

 1. **Verify as-is** — most code works with Verus directly.

18.    verifies the copy, not the real code.

20.    that still satisfies the spec, the spec is incomplete. A sorting spec
21.    that omits `is_sorted` passes a function that just copies the input.
22. 4. **Declarative, not operational** — a spec describes **what** must be true,
23.    not **how** the code achieves it. If you could swap quicksort for
24.    bubblesort and the spec still makes sense, it's a good spec.
25. 5. **Simpler than the code** — the spec should be at a higher level of
26.    abstraction than the implementation. For example, where the code has
27.    loops, the spec may use `forall`, `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` operations, or
28.    recursive spec functions.
29. 6. **Independent from the code** — two independent statements of the same truth.
30.    If derived by reading code line-by-line, it will reproduce bugs. A useful
31.    test: **could you have written this spec from just the function signature,
32.    type definitions, and module purpose — without reading the implementation?**

35.    over `u32`/`i32` (avoids overflow in specs), `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` over
36.    `Vec`/`HashMap`. Use `view()` / `self@` for abstract state. For pointer
37.    addresses, prefer `usize` over `int` — addresses are inherently
38.    non-negative and bounded by the address space.

40.    writing a caller's proof that uses this function. Would you use
41.    this fact as-is, or would you need to transform, combine, or
42.    unwrap it first? A good ensures clause is one the caller writes
43.    directly into their proof. Prefer vstd's existing spec functions
44.    (e.g., `self@.contains(x)`) over manual encodings (e.g.,
45.    `exists|i| ... && self@[i] == x`) — callers already reason with
46.    vstd APIs. On `exists`: valid when it genuinely hides
47.    implementation choice, but if the witness is computable from inputs
48.    and return values through the module's public spec interface,
49.    `exists` hides nothing — prefer a deterministic `let` binding.
50.

52. 
53. If exec functions have no `requires`/`ensures`, the result is a **desk reject**:
54. nothing was verified, regardless of how many spec functions or lemmas exist in

60.    module-level verification). If scope is unclear, default to all public

66.    functions that vstd does not cover. Never for workspace-internal code.

127.       explicitly in the spec.

129.       the API guarantees. Ask: "if I only read the doc (not the source
130.       code), would I believe this ensures clause is guaranteed?"

   physical address abstracts to the underlying virtual address's integer value.)
 - Assessment: clean slate. No upstream caller has biased the View yet; the inline
   `View::V = int` (raw address as a mathematical integer) is the natural starting point
   and is consistent with how callers use the type (see below).
 
 ## Trait Obligations
 
 `PhysicalAddress` implements:
 
 - `Address` (`from_raw_value`, `align_up`, `align_down`, `is_aligned`, `max_addr`,
   `into_raw_value`, `as_ptr`, `as_mut_ptr`) — generic address contract. Used by generic
   code such as `PageAligned<T: Address>` (`from_address`, `PartialEq`, `PartialOrd`),
   which is the primary indirect consumer of `is_aligned`/`into_raw_value`.

   and compare physical addresses and order them as raw integers.

   human-readable hex dump (logging in `book`, boot_init, `mod.rs`).
 
 Key trait-mediated expectation: `into_frame_number` / `from_number` and
 `PageAligned::from_address` together rely on the `Address::is_aligned` contract — a
 physical address built from a frame number is page-aligned, so wrapping it in

 ### `PhysicalAddress` (the type) — 76 references
 
 Representative callers: `mm/phys/frame.rs` (frame allocator: `book`, `is_covered`,
 `alloc_range` take `PageAligned<PhysicalAddress>` / `TruncatedMemoryRegion<PhysicalAddress>`),
 `mm/phys/mod.rs`, `kmod.rs` (stores `start` / `region_base` as `PhysicalAddress`),
 `hal/mem/types/address/frame.rs` (`FrameAddress` wraps `PageAligned<PhysicalAddress>`).
 
 - **Callers assume:**
   - It is a cheap `Copy` value that abstracts to a single integer (the raw physical
     address). Equality/ordering match integer equality/ordering of that raw value.
   - A `PhysicalAddress` that exists is a *valid* physical address (constructors enforce
     validity via `is_valid_physical_address`, except the explicitly-unsafe MMIO path).
   - Round-trips with `FrameNumber` and `usize` preserve the underlying value.
 - **Callers don't care about:**
   - That the inner representation is a `VirtualAddress` newtype. They never see the inner
     type; they go through `into_raw_value` / `into_virtual_address` / frame conversions.
   - Any platform-specific validity range internals.
 
 ### `from_number(frame: FrameNumber) -> Self`
 
 Sole caller: `hal/mem/types/address/frame.rs:78`
 `Ok(Self(PageAligned::from_address(PhysicalAddress::from_number(frame_number))?))`
 (inside `FrameAddress::from_frame_number`).
 
 - **Callers assume (success — infallible, returns `Self` not `Result`):**
   - The produced address equals `frame * FRAME_SIZE`, i.e. it is **page-aligned**. This
     is load-bearing: the caller immediately feeds the result to
     `PageAligned::from_address`, which calls `is_aligned(PAGE_ALIGNMENT)` and would error
     on a misaligned address. The caller propagates that `?` but in practice expects it to
     never trip for a frame-number-derived address.
   - The result is a valid, in-range physical address for any well-formed `FrameNumber`
     (`FrameNumber` is constructed only within `0..=MAX`, where `MAX = MAX_ADDRESS/FRAME_SIZE - 1`).
   - It is the inverse of `into_frame_number`: `from_number(f).into_frame_number() == f`.

     wraps a `VirtualAddress::new`.
 - **Would break the caller if changed:** returning a non-page-aligned address, or an
   address not equal to `frame * FRAME_SIZE` (breaks the `PageAligned` wrap and the
   round-trip with `into_frame_number`).
 
 ### `into_frame_number(self) -> FrameNumber`
 
 Callers (4):
 - `hal/mem/types/address/frame.rs:82` — `FrameAddress::into_frame_number` delegates.
 - `mm/phys/frame.rs:482` (`book`), `:518` (`is_covered`), `:569` (`alloc_range`):
   `let frame_number: usize = phys_addr.into_frame_number().into_raw_value();`
   then used to index a bitmap / refcount array.

   - It never panics for any `PhysicalAddress` that exists. The implementation `.unwrap()`s
     `FrameNumber::from_raw_value`; callers rely on the type invariant that a valid physical

     truncating any sub-frame offset. This is the abstract `view() / FRAME_SIZE`.
   - It is the inverse of `from_number` on page-aligned addresses; for the allocator,
     `phys_addr` arrives as `PageAligned<PhysicalAddress>`, so no offset is lost.

   - Whether it shifts or divides; only that the value is `floor(addr / FRAME_SIZE)`.

   returning a frame number not equal to `addr >> FRAME_SHIFT` (corrupts bitmap/refcount
   indexing → memory-safety bug in the frame allocator).

   `PhysicalAddress::from_mmio_address(VirtualAddress::from_raw_value(mmio_addr))?`.

     `book_mmio_regions` is explicit: "MMIO GPAs may legitimately lie outside tracked RAM,
     so they must not go through the regular physical-address validator here." This is the
     whole reason the function exists separately from `from_virtual_address` /
     `from_raw_value`.

     `addr` (identity wrap): `view() == addr@`.
   - The `unsafe` contract: the caller is responsible for the address actually denoting a
     valid MMIO region (callers acknowledge this with `// FIXME: ensure safety here.`).
   - Returns `Ok` for any input in current impl (it never actually errors), but callers
     still `?`-propagate to stay forward-compatible with a fallible signature.
 - **Callers don't care about:**
   - Internal representation; they immediately either page-align the result
     (`PageAligned::from_address`) or wrap it in a `FrameAddress`.
 - **Would break the caller if changed:** re-introducing the RAM-range validity check
   (would reject legitimate out-of-RAM MMIO frames and abort boot), or returning an address
   whose raw value differs from the input (breaks the GVA→GPA→frame mapping).
 
 ## Abstract Resource
 
 `PhysicalAddress` is a **validated handle to a single location in the host/guest physical

 the currency exchanged between the frame allocator, the paging/boot code, and frame-number

   equality/order on that value.

   (`== f * FRAME_SIZE`).
 - **Frame projection is total and offset-truncating:** `into_frame_number()` never panics
   for an existing address and yields `floor(view() / FRAME_SIZE)` (`view() >> FRAME_SHIFT`),
   a value always within `FrameNumber`'s valid range — directly usable as an allocator index.

   and performs no RAM-range validation.

233. ### `from_mmio_address(addr: VirtualAddress) -> Result<Self, Error>`  *(in scope, `unsafe`)*
234. 
235. ```text
236. ensures match result {
237.     Ok(r)  => r@ == addr@,   // identity wrapping; no RAM-range validation
238.     Err(_) => true,          // payload unconstrained; arm currently unreachable
239. }
240. ```
241. 
242. - **Identity, unchecked**: `Ok(r) => r@ == addr@`. This is the whole reason the
243.   function exists separately from `from_virtual_address` / `from_raw_value`: it
244.   **bypasses `is_valid_physical_address`**, so it succeeds for addresses the
245.   range-checked constructors reject. Returning an address whose raw value differs
246.   from the input, or re-introducing the RAM-range check, would break the
247.   GVA→GPA→frame mapping and abort boot — so the ensures pins identity and nothing
248.   more.
249. - **`unsafe` contract**: the caller promises the address denotes a valid MMIO GPA.
250.   That obligation underwrites `r.inv()` (frame-representability) so the result may
251.   later flow into `into_frame_number` via an `is_covered` gate; whether `inv()` is
252.   attached to the `Ok` arm as an ensures or discharged from the `unsafe`/`requires`
253.   precondition is settled in the spec phase. Using the `match` form keeps the
254.   success/failure spec complete by construction.
255. - **Error path**: the body is effectively `Ok(Self(addr))`, so `Err` never
256.   occurs; callers `?`-propagate to stay forward-compatible with the fallible
257.   signature and treat `Err` as a benign skip. The spec leaves the
258.   `Error`/`ErrorCode` payload unconstrained (callers never inspect it) rather than
259.   inventing a failure condition the implementation does not exhibit.

262. 
263. The type-level contract is precisely `inv()`: any `PhysicalAddress` value
264. produced by a verified constructor satisfies
265. `spec_frame_number(self@) <= spec_max_frame_number()`, and every in-scope
266. operation returning a `PhysicalAddress` preserves it. Holding the type is the
267. proof token that `into_frame_number` cannot panic; callers never re-check the
268. bound.

272. ## Design Rationale (substitution test per item)
273. 
274. > Test: *"If the implementation were completely rewritten with a different
275. > algorithm, would this still make sense?"*
276. 
277. | Item | Meaning | Substitution test |
278. |------|---------|-------------------|
279. | `self@ : int` (raw address) | The numeric physical address the handle denotes. | **Passes.** Whether `PhysicalAddress` is a newtype over `VirtualAddress`, a bare `usize`, or a struct with tag bits, "the integer physical address" is the one quantity every caller reasons about — frame indexing, ordering, equality, MMIO identity, raw round-trips. The `closed` view hides *how* the int is stored. |
280. | `spec_frame_number(self@)` (derived helper) | The frame the address lies in. | **Passes.** Derived purely from `self@` and the module constant; any implementation that means "frame number" by `addr >> FRAME_SHIFT` computes `addr / FRAME_SIZE`, regardless of shift-vs-divide. Not stored, so no rewrite can desync it. |
281. | `inv()` = frame-representable | The frame index fits a `FrameNumber`. | **Passes.** A property of the *abstract value*, not of any storage layout. Any implementation must maintain it for `into_frame_number` to be total; it is the universal precondition the allocator relies on. |
282. 
283. Why these and not more:
284. 
285. - **Caller-only**: each item is understandable from the function signatures and
286.   the caller analysis alone — none requires reading a function body.
287. - **Complete**: the View + helper + `inv()` cover every caller-observable concept
288.   in the analysis — the address value (`self@`), the frame number
289.   (`spec_frame_number`), totality of `into_frame_number` (`inv()`), the
290.   `from_number` alignment-of-base fact (a *consequence* of its ensures), and MMIO
291.   identity (`r@ == addr@`).
292. - **Minimal**: each item is used by at least one in-scope contract; the View is a
293.   single scalar with no redundant or derivable stored state.
294. 
295. Why `closed view` + `open inv`:
296. 
297. - `view()` is **closed** so the newtype delegation to `VirtualAddress` does not
298.   leak; callers still get a usable `int` for arithmetic and comparison.
299. - `inv()` is **open** because the frame-representability fact is the public
300.   promise callers must unfold to discharge `into_frame_number`'s `requires`.
301. 
302. Consistency with siblings: the entire `hal::mem` address family —
303. `VirtualAddress`, `PageAligned<T>`, `FrameAddress`, and `arch`'s `FrameNumber` —
304. uses `type V = int` with a `closed` newtype-identity `view`. Mirroring it keeps
305. the tower uniform so `PhysicalAddress`'s contracts compose directly with
306. `FrameAddress::from_frame_number` / `into_frame_number` (which delegate straight
307. through `from_number` / `into_frame_number`) and with `PageAligned::from_address`.
308. 
309. ---
310. 
311. ## Rejected Alternatives
312. 
313. 1. **A struct View `{ addr: int, frame: int }`.** Rejected. `frame` is a pure
314.    function of `addr` (`addr / spec_page_size()`); storing it duplicates state,
315.    forces a redundant `inv()` consistency clause, and fails minimality. Kept as
316.    the derived helper `spec_frame_number(self@)` instead.
317. 
318. 2. **Exposing the inner `VirtualAddress`** (`type V = VirtualAddress`, or a field
319.    for it). Rejected. The caller analysis is explicit that the `VirtualAddress`
320.    wrapper is an implementation detail; only the integer matters. Mirroring it
321.    violates the cardinal rule (don't mirror internal fields), leaks the storage
322.    choice (fails Substitution / Caller-only), and forces callers through `T`'s API
323.    to recover the number they actually want.
324. 
325. 3. **An alignment invariant `self@ % spec_page_size() == 0`** (as on
326.    `PageAligned`/`FrameAddress`). Rejected as a *type* invariant.
327.    `from_mmio_address` legitimately produces unaligned addresses, so alignment
328.    cannot hold for all `PhysicalAddress` values. It is captured where it actually
329.    holds — as a *consequence* of `from_number`'s ensures.
330. 
331. 4. **A RAM-range invariant `is_valid_physical_address(self@)`.** Rejected.
332.    `from_mmio_address` deliberately bypasses RAM validation for MMIO regions
333.    outside tracked RAM, so this is false for valid MMIO `PhysicalAddress` values.
334.    The weaker frame-representability bound is the property that is both
335.    universally true and sufficient for the totality obligation.
336.

338.    `.unwrap()`s `FrameNumber::from_raw_value`; without an upper bound on the frame
339.    index the totality / no-panic guarantee the frame allocator depends on cannot
340.    be proven. Frame-representability is the minimal bound that discharges it.

345.    `spec_frame_number(self@)` in the ensures, keeping the View a single scalar.

 ensures match result {
     Ok(r)  => r@ == addr@,   // identity wrapping; no RAM-range validation

   occurs; callers `?`-propagate to stay forward-compatible with the fallible

   `Error`/`ErrorCode` payload unconstrained (callers never inspect it) rather than
   inventing a failure condition the implementation does not exhibit.

 proof token that `into_frame_number` cannot panic; callers never re-check the

 > Test: *"If the implementation were completely rewritten with a different
 > algorithm, would this still make sense?"*
 
 | Item | Meaning | Substitution test |
 |------|---------|-------------------|
 | `self@ : int` (raw address) | The numeric physical address the handle denotes. | **Passes.** Whether `PhysicalAddress` is a newtype over `VirtualAddress`, a bare `usize`, or a struct with tag bits, "the integer physical address" is the one quantity every caller reasons about — frame indexing, ordering, equality, MMIO identity, raw round-trips.  | `spec_frame_number(self@)` (derived helper) | The frame the address lies in. | **Passes.** Derived purely from `self@` and the module constant; any implementation that means "frame number" by `addr >> FRAME_SHIFT` computes `addr / FRAME_SIZE`, regardless of shift-vs-divide.  - **Caller-only**: each item is understandable from the function signatures and
   the caller analysis alone — none requires reading a function body.
 - **Complete**: the View + helper + `inv()` cover every caller-observable concept
   in the analysis — the address value (`self@`), the frame number
   (`spec_frame_number`), totality of `into_frame_number` (`inv()`), the
   `from_number` alignment-of-base fact (a *consequence* of its ensures), and MMIO
   identity (`r@ == addr@`).
 - **Minimal**: each item is used by at least one in-scope contract; the View is a
   single scalar with no redundant or derivable stored state.

   leak; callers still get a usable `int` for arithmetic and comparison.

   promise callers must unfold to discharge `into_frame_number`'s `requires`.

 `VirtualAddress`, `PageAligned<T>`, `FrameAddress`, and `arch`'s `FrameNumber` —

 `FrameAddress::from_frame_number` / `into_frame_number` (which delegate straight
 through `from_number` / `into_frame_number`) and with `PageAligned::from_address`.
 
 ---
 
 ## Rejected Alternatives
 
 1. **A struct View `{ addr: int, frame: int }`.** Rejected. `frame` is a pure
    function of `addr` (`addr / spec_page_size()`); storing it duplicates state,
    forces a redundant `inv()` consistency clause, and fails minimality. Kept as
    the derived helper `spec_frame_number(self@)` instead.
 
 2. **Exposing the inner `VirtualAddress`** (`type V = VirtualAddress`, or a field
    for it). Rejected. The caller analysis is explicit that the `VirtualAddress`
    wrapper is an implementation detail; only the integer matters. Mirroring it
    violates the cardinal rule (don't mirror internal fields), leaks the storage
    choice (fails Substitution / Caller-only), and forces callers through `T`'s API
    to recover the number they actually want.
 
 3. **An alignment invariant `self@ % spec_page_size() == 0`** (as on
    `PageAligned`/`FrameAddress`). Rejected as a *type* invariant.
    `from_mmio_address` legitimately produces unaligned addresses, so alignment
    cannot hold for all `PhysicalAddress` values. It is captured where it actually
    holds — as a *consequence* of `from_number`'s ensures.
 
 4. **A RAM-range invariant `is_valid_physical_address(self@)`.** Rejected.
    `from_mmio_address` deliberately bypasses RAM validation for MMIO regions
    outside tracked RAM, so this is false for valid MMIO `PhysicalAddress` values.
    The weaker frame-representability bound is the property that is both
    universally true and sufficient for the totality obligation.
 
 5. **No invariant at all (`inv() == true`).** Rejected. `into_frame_number`
    `.unwrap()`s `FrameNumber::from_raw_value`; without an upper bound on the frame
    index the totality / no-panic guarantee the frame allocator depends on cannot
    be proven. Frame-representability is the minimal bound that discharges it.
 
 6. **Modeling `into_frame_number`'s result as an `int` field in the View.** N/A
    as a View field — there is no second piece of state. The relation is expressed
    by tying the returned `FrameNumber`'s index (`spec_frame_raw_value(result)`) to
    `spec_frame_number(self@)` in the ensures, keeping the View a single scalar.
 
 7. **A `nat` (or `usize`) View instead of `int`.** Rejected. `nat`/`usize`

    everywhere), forcing `nat`/`int` coercions in cross-type lemmas, and `usize`
    reintroduces overflow reasoning into specs. Non-negativity (`0 <= self@`) holds
    structurally (the view comes from a `usize`) and is recorded in `inv()` where
    needed; `int` is the consistent, cast-free choice.

 |-----------|--------|
 | **Substitution** | The single field (`addr : int`) and the derived helper / `inv()` survive any reimplementation; storage layout (newtype-over-`VirtualAddress`) is invisible. ✅ |

 | **Minimal** | One scalar field; `view()`, `inv()`, and each helper are used by an in-scope contract. No unused or derivable stored state. ✅ |

 ```rust

 //   spec_max_frame_number() : int                           // == FrameNumber::MAX
 //   spec_frame_raw_value(frame: FrameNumber) -> int         // frame's index

51. caller-observable quantity. The existing inline skeleton is **kept unchanged**:

54. impl View for PhysicalAddress {
55.     type V = int;
56. 
57.     // `closed`: callers may reference `self@`, but the mapping to the inner
58.     // VirtualAddress field is hidden. The abstract value is "the physical
59.     // address as an unbounded integer".
60.     closed spec fn view(&self) -> int {
61.         self.0@      // newtype identity: delegate to the inner address's view
62.     }
63. }
64. ```
65. 
66. `self@ : int` is the entire abstract state. This mirrors the rest of the address
67. tower — `VirtualAddress@ : int`, `PageAligned<T>@ : int`, `FrameAddress@ : int`,
68. `FrameNumber@ : int` — confirming the abstraction is caller-driven, not
69. implementation-driven: every member models a value as a single `int`.
70. 
71. `view()` is **`closed`** so the newtype delegation (`self.0@`) does not leak the
72. `VirtualAddress` representation; callers still obtain a usable `int` (`p@`) for
73. arithmetic, frame indexing, and comparison.

76. 
77. ```rust
78. pub struct PhysicalAddressView {
79.     // addr: the numeric physical address this handle denotes, as `int`.
80.     //       The only state a caller can observe. The "frame it lies in" is a
81.     //       *derived* quantity (addr / FRAME_SIZE), not a stored field;
82.     //       in-range-ness is a *property* of this value, expressed by inv().
83.     addr: int,
84. }

88.

90. named helper over the abstract `int` rather than a stored field:
91.

94. // `addr >> FRAME_SHIFT`, stated as exact integer division so the spec is
95. // independent of shift-vs-divide.
96. pub open spec fn spec_frame_number(addr_view: int) -> int {
97.     addr_view / spec_page_size()
98. }
99. ```
100. 
101. `spec_page_size() : int` is the pre-existing uninterpreted module constant tied
102. to `FRAME_SIZE`/`PAGE_SIZE` (the caller analysis establishes
103. `FRAME_SIZE == spec_page_size()`). `spec_max_frame_number() : int` denotes

107. `FrameNumber` type at the `phys.spec.rs` edge, and they are the vocabulary the
108. `from_number` / `into_frame_number` contracts use.
109. 
110. ---
111. 
112. ## Well-formedness Invariant
113. 
114. `PhysicalAddress` carries **one** universal property that every constructible
115. value satisfies and that callers depend on: its address has a **representable
116. frame number**. This is exactly the fact that makes `into_frame_number` total —
117. its internal `FrameNumber::from_raw_value(addr >> FRAME_SHIFT).unwrap()` never
118. panics — which the frame allocator relies on to use the result directly as a
119. bitmap / refcount index without a bounds re-check.
120.

122. impl PhysicalAddress {
123.     // `open`: the frame allocator and page-table code rely on the totality of
124.     // into_frame_number, so the underwriting fact must be visible in their
125.     // proofs (not hidden behind a closed predicate).
126.     pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
127.         // 0 <= self@ holds structurally (the view comes from a usize); the

129.         spec_frame_number(self@) <= spec_max_frame_number()

136. (`== self@ < MAX_ADDRESS`). Both express the same caller-visible guarantee: the

154.   sit far below the top of the address space, so the bound holds for them in

216.          // == self@ / spec_page_size()   (equivalently self@ >> FRAME_SHIFT)
217. ```

219. - **Total under `inv()`**: the receiver's invariant
220.   (`spec_frame_number(self@) <= spec_max_frame_number()`) guarantees the computed

     closed spec fn view(&self) -> int {
         self.0@      // newtype identity: delegate to the inner address's view
     }
 }
 ```
 
 `self@ : int` is the entire abstract state. This mirrors the rest of the address
 tower — `VirtualAddress@ : int`, `PageAligned<T>@ : int`, `FrameAddress@ : int`,
 `FrameNumber@ : int` — confirming the abstraction is caller-driven, not
 implementation-driven: every member models a value as a single `int`.
 
 `view()` is **`closed`** so the newtype delegation (`self.0@`) does not leak the
 `VirtualAddress` representation; callers still obtain a usable `int` (`p@`) for
 arithmetic, frame indexing, and comparison.
 
 ### Equivalent "single-field" reading
 
 ```rust
 pub struct PhysicalAddressView {
     // addr: the numeric physical address this handle denotes, as `int`.
     //       The only state a caller can observe. The "frame it lies in" is a
     //       *derived* quantity (addr / FRAME_SIZE), not a stored field;
     //       in-range-ness is a *property* of this value, expressed by inv().
     addr: int,
 }
 ```
 
 ### Derived spec helper (over the View domain)
 
 The frame index is the single derived quantity callers reason about, so it gets a
 named helper over the abstract `int` rather than a stored field:
 
 ```rust
 // The frame that this physical address belongs to. Equals the implementation's
 // `addr >> FRAME_SHIFT`, stated as exact integer division so the spec is
 // independent of shift-vs-divide.
 pub open spec fn spec_frame_number(addr_view: int) -> int {
     addr_view / spec_page_size()
 }
 ```
 
 `spec_page_size() : int` is the pre-existing uninterpreted module constant tied
 to `FRAME_SIZE`/`PAGE_SIZE` (the caller analysis establishes
 `FRAME_SIZE == spec_page_size()`). `spec_max_frame_number() : int` denotes
 `FrameNumber::MAX` (`= MAX_ADDRESS / FRAME_SIZE - 1`); together with
 `spec_frame_raw_value(frame: FrameNumber) -> int` (the frame's integer index)
 these are the trust-boundary helpers that pin the not-yet-verified `arch`
 `FrameNumber` type at the `phys.spec.rs` edge, and they are the vocabulary the
 `from_number` / `into_frame_number` contracts use.
 
 ---
 
 ## Well-formedness Invariant
 
 `PhysicalAddress` carries **one** universal property that every constructible
 value satisfies and that callers depend on: its address has a **representable
 frame number**. This is exactly the fact that makes `into_frame_number` total —
 its internal `FrameNumber::from_raw_value(addr >> FRAME_SHIFT).unwrap()` never
 panics — which the frame allocator relies on to use the result directly as a
 bitmap / refcount index without a bounds re-check.
 
 ```rust
 impl PhysicalAddress {
     // `open`: the frame allocator and page-table code rely on the totality of
     // into_frame_number, so the underwriting fact must be visible in their
     // proofs (not hidden behind a closed predicate).
     pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
         // 0 <= self@ holds structurally (the view comes from a usize); the
         // operative bound is that the frame index fits a FrameNumber.
         spec_frame_number(self@) <= spec_max_frame_number()
     }
 }
 ```
 
 The exact integer form is finalized in the spec phase; the equivalent address-space
 phrasing is `0 <= self@ < (spec_max_frame_number() + 1) * spec_page_size()`
 (`== self@ < MAX_ADDRESS`). Both express the same caller-visible guarantee: the
 address lies within the representable physical address space, so its frame index
 is a valid `FrameNumber`.
 
 **Why frame-representability and *not* alignment or RAM-validity.**
 
 - Unlike `PageAligned`/`FrameAddress`, `PhysicalAddress` does **not** carry an
   alignment invariant: `from_mmio_address` deliberately wraps arbitrary,
   possibly-unaligned MMIO addresses (e.g. the LAPIC base `0xFEE0_0000`). Alignment
   is a property of *specific* constructors (`from_number`), not of the type.
 - It does **not** carry a tracked-RAM-validity invariant
   (`is_valid_physical_address(self@)`) either: `from_mmio_address` exists
   precisely to bypass the RAM-range validator, since "MMIO GPAs may legitimately
   lie outside tracked RAM." A RAM-validity invariant would be *false* for valid
   MMIO `PhysicalAddress` values.
 - Frame-representability is the **weakest property that is both universally true
   (across every constructor, including the unsafe MMIO path) and strong enough**
   for the one totality obligation the in-scope functions impose. Real MMIO GPAs
   sit far below the top of the address space, so the bound holds for them in
   practice; the `unsafe` contract of `from_mmio_address` underwrites it for the
   result.
 
 `inv()` is `pub open` because callers must unfold it to discharge
 `into_frame_number`'s `requires`. `internal_inv()` is not needed at this phase:
 there is no redundant/derived exec field to keep consistent (the View has one
 scalar, mapped by `closed view` to the single inner field); the specification
 phase may introduce one if impl bodies reveal a consistency obligation, in which
 case `inv()` would conjoin `self.internal_inv()`.
 
 ---
 
 ## Spec Transition Functions
 
 `PhysicalAddress` is an **immutable value type**: the in-scope functions are pure
 constructors / projections, so there is no mutable pre/post state machine. The
 "transitions" are deterministic relations between input views and the resulting
 abstract value, stated over the View's `int` domain. They are given below as the
 contracts the spec phase will attach to the exec functions (no extra `pub spec
 fn` is added to `impl PhysicalAddress` beyond `inv`, per the view-design rule —
 the reusable helpers live on the View domain).
 
 ```rust
 // Base address of a frame: from_number multiplies the frame index by the frame
 // size. Stated as multiplication, independent of the body's shift-vs-mul.
 pub open spec fn spec_from_number(frame_view: int) -> int {
     frame_view * spec_page_size()
 }
 ```
 
 ### `from_number(frame: FrameNumber) -> Self`  *(in scope — total constructor)*
 
 ```text
 ensures
     result@ == spec_from_number(spec_frame_raw_value(frame))
     //       == spec_frame_raw_value(frame) * spec_page_size()
     // hence result@ % spec_page_size() == 0   (frame-aligned base address)
     // and   result.inv()                      (frame index == frame <= MAX)
 ```
 
 - **Total** (returns `Self`, not `Result`): every `FrameNumber` yields a
   `PhysicalAddress`, as the sole caller (`FrameAddress::from_frame_number`)
   assumes.
 - **Value relation, not mechanism**: the result is the frame's base address. The
   caller immediately feeds it to `PageAligned::from_address(..)?`, which calls
   `is_aligned(PAGE_ALIGNMENT)`; this `?` is load-bearing, so the alignment fact
   `result@ % spec_page_size() == 0` must *follow* from the ensures. It does,
   because `result@` is `frame_index * spec_page_size()`. Both alignment and
   `inv()` are consequences of this single ensures (since
   `spec_frame_raw_value(frame) <= spec_max_frame_number()` for any well-formed
   `FrameNumber`), so they are **not** listed as separate clauses (avoids subsumed
   properties).
 - **Inverse of `into_frame_number`**: `from_number(f).into_frame_number()` yields
   a frame whose index equals `spec_frame_raw_value(f)` — provable from this
   ensures plus `into_frame_number`'s.
 
 ### `into_frame_number(self) -> FrameNumber`  *(in scope — total projection)*
 
 ```text
 requires self.inv()                 // underwrites totality of the internal unwrap
 ensures  spec_frame_raw_value(result) == spec_frame_number(self@)
          // == self@ / spec_page_size()   (equivalently self@ >> FRAME_SHIFT)
 ```
 
 - **Total under `inv()`**: the receiver's invariant
   (`spec_frame_number(self@) <= spec_max_frame_number()`) guarantees the computed

   bridges the live `Inner` to the abstract `phys_view().frames`.

 `free_frames.len() + usage == num_bits` without any `admit()`.

 `alloc_range`, `share`) are body-verified and carry the **strong** post-state

 both `old(auth)@` (pre-state) and `final(auth)@` (post-state) and asserts the

 precondition-free for `Drop` soundness. The function is therefore `external_body`
 with its weak, always-true `ensures phys_view().inv()` honored as a trust boundary

 `proof! { admit(); }`; the trust surface is identical, but `external_body` is the
 governed mechanism. It is the single deliberate, caller-justified `Drop`-path
 exception — **not** the forbidden weakening, which concerned the reservation ops
 that now carry the strong `PhysAuth`-threaded post-state.
 
 - `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs::free` — releases one reference on `Drop`.
   `ensures phys_view().inv()` on every path; no precondition (`Drop`-safe).

   `Alignment` are verified.

   `external_type_specification` wrapper registering the foreign `arch::FrameNumber`
   as opaque. No body verified; carries no abstract guarantee beyond opacity.

1. ---
2. name: spec-design
3. description: "How to write good Verus specs. Covers spec quality principles (anti-patterns, error paths), spec classification (internal, external-top, external-bottom trust boundaries), View abstraction design, and static vs dynamic enforcement. Use when writing or reviewing Verus specs."
4. ---
5. 
6. # Spec Design Guide
7. 
8. ## Part 1: Spec Quality Principles
9. 
10. ### Qualities of a Good Spec
11. 
12. 1. **Bound to exec code** — every property must appear as `requires`,
13.    `ensures`, or loop `invariant` on an exec function. Standalone spec
14.    functions that no exec function references prove nothing.
15. 2. **Annotates the original** — specs are added directly to the original
16.    exec function using `#[verus_spec]` (see `verus-syntax` skill). Never
17.    copy exec functions into a `verus!{}` block and spec the copy — that
18.    verifies the copy, not the real code.
19. 3. **Sufficient to reject bugs** — if you can imagine a buggy implementation
20.    that still satisfies the spec, the spec is incomplete. A sorting spec
21.    that omits `is_sorted` passes a function that just copies the input.
22. 4. **Declarative, not operational** — a spec describes **what** must be true,
23.    not **how** the code achieves it. If you could swap quicksort for
24.    bubblesort and the spec still makes sense, it's a good spec.
25. 5. **Simpler than the code** — the spec should be at a higher level of
26.    abstraction than the implementation. For example, where the code has
27.    loops, the spec may use `forall`, `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` operations, or
28.    recursive spec functions.
29. 6. **Independent from the code** — two independent statements of the same truth.
30.    If derived by reading code line-by-line, it will reproduce bugs. A useful
31.    test: **could you have written this spec from just the function signature,
32.    type definitions, and module purpose — without reading the implementation?**
33.    If not, the spec likely mirrors the code rather than abstracting over it.
34. 7. **Uses mathematical objects where they simplify reasoning** — prefer `int`
35.    over `u32`/`i32` (avoids overflow in specs), `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` over
36.    `Vec`/`HashMap`. Use `view()` / `self@` for abstract state. For pointer
37.    addresses, prefer `usize` over `int` — addresses are inherently
38.    non-negative and bounded by the address space.
39. 8. **Written for the caller** — for each ensures clause, simulate
40.    writing a caller's proof that uses this function. Would you use
41.    this fact as-is, or would you need to transform, combine, or
42.    unwrap it first? A good ensures clause is one the caller writes
43.    directly into their proof. Prefer vstd's existing spec functions
44.    (e.g., `self@.contains(x)`) over manual encodings (e.g.,
45.    `exists|i| ... && self@[i] == x`) — callers already reason with
46.    vstd APIs. On `exists`: valid when it genuinely hides
47.    implementation choice, but if the witness is computable from inputs
48.    and return values through the module's public spec interface,
49.    `exists` hides nothing — prefer a deterministic `let` binding.
50. 
51. ### Exec Binding Rules — Desk Reject Criteria
52. 
53. If exec functions have no `requires`/`ensures`, the result is a **desk reject**:
54. nothing was verified, regardless of how many spec functions or lemmas exist in
55. spec.rs/proof.rs. Our goal is a **verified implementation**, not a verified
56. design model.
57. 
58. 1. **Every exec function in scope gets contracts** — "in scope" is determined
59.    by the verification task (e.g., caller analysis, human directive, or
60.    module-level verification). If scope is unclear, default to all public
61.    and safety-critical functions. No annotation is a desk reject; partial
62.    annotation beats no annotation.
63. 2. **Search vstd before writing `assume_specification`** — vstd already
64.    provides specs for many std library functions. Only write
65.    `assume_specification` for std library or third-party dependency
66.    functions that vstd does not cover. Never for workspace-internal code.
67.    Always search vstd first.
68. 3. **Reuse dependency specs** — before calling a function from another
69.    module in the project, search for its `.spec.rs`:
70.    `find . -name "*.spec.rs" | head -20`. If the dependency has verified
71.    specs, import and use them directly. If it does not, add `#[verus_spec]`
72.    annotations on the dependency function — do NOT use `assume_specification`
73.    for project-internal code (any crate in the workspace). `assume_specification`
74.    is only for third-party dependencies and std library functions not covered
75.    by vstd.
76.    **Why this works without `admit()`**: `--verify-module M` only verifies
77.    functions in module M. Specs on functions in other modules are treated as
78.    trusted contracts — their bodies are not checked. When those modules are
79.    verified later, the specs become fully proven.
80. 5. **No floating specs** — every spec function and lemma must ultimately
81.    connect to an exec contract. Orphan specs are dead code.
82. 6. **No `external_body` on current module** — the current module's functions
83.    must never be marked `external_body`. Use `admit()` in proof bodies to
84.    make Verus pass.
85.    **Dependency functions** in other modules may be marked `external_body`
86.    with `requires`/`ensures` to provide contracts that the current module
87.    can rely on. These are removed when the dependency module is verified.
88. 
89. ### Anti-Patterns (reject or remove)
90. 
91. 1. **Exec Code Mutation** — modifying existing exec code, APIs, or
92.    struct definitions to accommodate specs. Do not change function
93.    signatures, alter control flow, or add exec fields to structs.
94.    Adding `Ghost<T>` / `Tracked<T>` fields is allowed — they are
95.    erased at compile time and do not change exec behavior. However,
96.    prefer keeping ghost state in spec.rs (e.g., on the View type)
97.    rather than adding fields to exec structs; only add when the proof
98.    genuinely requires ghost state to flow through exec code.
99.    
100.    Exec code must NOT be changed — the code has been pre-refactored to be
101.    fully Verus-compatible. See `verus-constraints` skill.
102. 2. **Verification Escape** — using `assume`, `admit`,
103.    or `exec_allows_no_decreases_clause` to bypass verification. Fix the
104.    spec or proof instead.
105.    
106.    **Exceptions (legitimate trust boundaries):**
107.    - `assume_specification`: for std library / external functions whose
108.      source code is outside the verification scope (e.g., not in our
109.      crate). Write the spec to match the original API documentation.
110. 
111.    **assume_specification Audit Checklist:**
112. 
113.    1. **Read the official docs first**: find the function's doc comments
114.       in `~/.rustup/toolchains/*/lib/rustlib/src/rust/library/` using
115.       `grep -rn "fn <name>"`. Write the spec from these docs, not from
116.       reading the implementation or copying an internal helper's spec.
117.       Capture all documented semantics, including implicit type
118.       requirements (e.g., trait bounds imply properties like total ordering).
119.    2. **Documentation fidelity**: every ensures clause must be explicitly
120.       guaranteed by the original API documentation. If the doc does not
121.       guarantee it, mark the clause as "assumed beyond documentation".
122.       Conversely, every documented precondition must appear as a `requires`
123.       clause — omitting a precondition makes the spec unsound because
124.       callers will not check it.
125.    3. **Soft contract coverage**: identify semantic contracts that the
126.       compiler does not enforce but the API requires. Express these
127.       explicitly in the spec.
128.    4. **No stronger than the API**: the spec must not assume more than
129.       the API guarantees. Ask: "if I only read the doc (not the source
130.       code), would I believe this ensures clause is guaranteed?"
131.    5. **Version sensitivity**: note the stdlib/crate version the
132.       assumption was checked against.
133. 
134.    - `external_body`: allowed on dependency functions in other modules as
135.      a temporary contract placeholder (removed when that module is verified),
136.      and on functions pre-approved in the TCB allowed list.
137.      Never use `external_body` on the current module's own functions to skip
138.      verification.
139.    
140.    `assume_specification` and `axiom` are unverified axioms.
141.    See the audit checklist above when writing `assume_specification`.
142. 3. **Missing Loop Specs** — loops need `invariant` clauses that capture
143.    the loop's progress and preservation properties. A function with
144.    loops but no loop invariants has an incomplete spec. Verus will reject
145.    it. For complex invariants, define a `spec fn` predicate in spec.rs
146.    or proof.rs and reference it in the `invariant` clause. The invariant
147.    must be strong enough that, combined with the loop exit condition, it
148.    implies the function's `ensures`. The invariant may need to be
149.    strengthened later — that is expected.
150. 4. **Code-as-Spec / Operational Spec** — restating implementation logic
151.    or describing computation step-by-step. Bad: recursive quicksort in
152.    spec. Good: `is_sorted(result@) && is_permutation_of(result@, input@)`.
153. 5. **One-Sided Error Spec** — only specifies success, says nothing

161.    ```
162.    self@.field_a == old(self)@.field_a,
163.    self@.field_b == old(self)@.field_b,
164.    self@.field_c == new_value,
165.    // forgot field_d — spec is incomplete!
166.    ```
167.    Good (complete by construction):
168.    ```
169.    self@ == ViewType { field_c: new_value, ..old(self)@ }
170.    ```
